16331-new-york-times-current-history-the:
This volume of New York Times Current History gathers documents and comment from the European War's first months. A statement approved by Dr. Dernburg, dated November 1, 1914, argues that Austria-Hungary and Russia, whose differences sharpened for years, made the struggle unavoidable after the Sarajevo tragedy. Germany and France, tied by alliances, joined them, while Italy and England, each tied to one side yet removed from the continent, faced uncertain choices.

Current History gave American readers the war in documents, maps, and essays as it unfolded. The volume preserves German, Allied, and neutral voices side by side. Students of the First World War will find a valuable contemporary record of how the war was explained.
23646-the-pharaoh-and-the-priest-an-hist:
Alexander Glovatski's historical novel of ancient Egypt reached English readers in 1902 through Jeremiah Curtin, translator of Quo Vadis and With Fire and Sword. Its setting is the Nile valley, where every acre of rich soil was laid down by river mud from inner Africa, and where grain from Egyptian fields fed Rome, Greece, and Judaea.

That wealth could only be worked by a whole people directed together. The novel's conflict grows from that fact: the pharaoh and the priesthood, the two powers that commanded the land's labor, contend for control of Egypt. Curtin prefaces the tale with an essay on Egypt's unique place, making this both a romance of the ancient world and a study of power built on the river.
30772-minutes-of-the-proceedings-of-the-:
Held here are the minutes of the second convention of delegates from the abolition societies of the United States, held at Philadelphia from January 7 to January 14, 1795. Printed by Zachariah Poulson Jr. on Chestnut Street, the minutes open at City Hall on Wednesday, January 7, 1795, following a convention held in the city the year before. Delegates came with credentials from societies across the young republic.

Connecticut sent Jonathan Edwards, Uriah Tracy, and Zephaniah Swift, while New York and Pennsylvania sent men such as William Rawle, Benjamin Rush, Samuel Coates, and Caspar Wistar. The minutes record who sat, what was moved, and how the societies joined their efforts against slavery. It is a primary source for early American abolition, plain in form and rich in names and dates.
31315-charles-sumner-centenary-historica:
Archibald H. Grimké's 1911 address, number fourteen in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, marks the centenary of Charles Sumner. The Academy celebrated on Friday evening, January 6, 1911, at Washington's Fifteenth Street Presbyterian Church, with a choir singing A Mighty Fortress, an invocation by the Reverend L. Z. Johnson, Grimké's historical address, a brief address by Justice Wendell Phillips Stafford, a solo by Dr. Charles Sumner Wormley, an address by Vice-President Kelly Miller, a poem by Mrs. F. J. Grimke, and a closing address by William E. Chandler.

Grimké opens with the fable of Hercules receiving sword, bow, breastplate, and robe from the gods, arguing Sumner likewise drew strength from many sources. Sumner loved the science of law rather than its practice, thirsting for permanent principles in Grotius, Pothier, Mansfield, and Blackstone. The address honors a statesman as the Academy's own hero.
31323-the-demand-and-the-supply-of-incre:
Jesse E. Moorland's 1909 paper, number thirteen in the American Negro Academy's Occasional Papers, argues for a greater number of efficient ministers. Moorland concedes a Christian lawyer or doctor holds as genuine a divine calling as any minister, with such men stressing service over gain. He calls the minister's efficiency probably the most important question confronting colored people.

A race or nation, he argues, is measured by its religion, and the Negro minister has been responsible both for the race's progress and for much that cannot count as progress. No other class, he notes, holds so large and far-reaching an influence. The paper tells the familiar anecdote of Queen Victoria holding up the Bible as the secret of Britain's greatness, and pleads for well-trained, honorable, upright ministers in every community.
35061-two-years-on-trek-being-some-accou:
Du Moulin, a late Sussex chief, told of two years on trek in South Africa. Panton wrote the front words, and Bidder shaped the book. It came out in 1907 from Brompton Road in London. His mates made the book a shrine to a brave man, the front says. Sweet and fit to die for one's land, its Latin line claims.

To Bloemfontein leads the trek, and a brigade starts it there. Zand River, its fight, and the Vaal's cross fill the front parts. Doornkop and Pretoria's fall mark the march's high span. Diamond Hill's two days of fight stand in the mid list. Springs and Reitz close this part of the long road. War fans get a corps tale.
35499-the-pharaoh-and-the-priest-an-hist:
Pharaoh and the Priest is a historical novel of ancient Egypt. Alexander Glovatski wrote it in Polish, and Jeremiah Curtin translated it. Little, Brown and Company published it in Boston in the year 1902. Curtin also translated With Fire and Sword, The Deluge, and Quo Vadis. Photographs illustrate the volume, with Curtin shown at Luxor by Rameses.

Prefatory remarks call the position of ancient Egypt unique in every sense. Each acre of fruitful land, Curtin says, came down from Inner Africa. The Nile laid that soil between the first cataract and the sea. Fresh silt added to it year by year in flood season. Priest and pharaoh contend for Egypt in the tale that follows.
39898-western-scenes-and-reminiscences-t:
Western Scenes and Reminiscences came out at Auburn and Buffalo in 1853. Its entry was made in 1851 by the Derby house, the front says. Thrilling legends and traditions of the red men stand in the title. Several narratives of adventures among the Indians are added to it. A plate shows a captive tortured, in the old frontier mode.

Contents open with personal reminiscences and Ozark Mountain scenes. Personal incidents and impressions of the Indian race follow in the book. Tales of a wigwam then gather the native legends in a row. The white stone canoe, the lynx and the hare, and sun worship stand there. Shingebiss, the boy who set a snare for the sun, and the toad woman follow. Machinito the evil spirit and a little spirit tale close the gathering. The book mixes settler memory with Odjibwa and Ottawa lore.
49427-consecrated-womanhood-a-sermon-pre:
Consecrated Womanhood is a church talk by Frederic Rowland Marvin, out in print in nineteen three. Marvin gave the talk at a church in Portland, on the far west coast. Five hundred copies of this form were struck from type in one month. A front note by Frances Power Cobbe, a famed hand for the rights of wives, leads the book.

Cobbe calls the talk a breath of fresh air for those who mourn that churches bar wives from high church posts. The talk opens with the claim that the old book gave wives grace when all else was blind to their worth. She adds that the Greek stage set its best types in wives, and that the old Jews stood not alone in that grace.
51320-break-a-leg:
Jim Harmon wrote the tale Break A Leg for Galaxy. The magazine ran it in November 1957. Gaughan drew its pictures for the issue. A captain tells the tale in first person. Rookie Accident Prones aboard ship scare him stiff. Such men starve in unemployment lines ashore, he says.

Prone men please eagerly to keep their berths, he notes. Day-old bread was their shore fare, he recalls. Steak and caviar greet them in the Exploration Service. A Prone trips over his own feet in a block. Cars and live wires thin their ranks ashore. The Admiralty uses their curse as a tool, he explains. A Prone finds a planet's dangers by falling in. One pit of quicksand draws him knee-deep, he says. A wry space tale makes the born loser the fleet's best safety tester, one fall at a time.
55087-historical-record-of-the-forty-six:
Historical Record of the Forty Sixth Regiment traces a British foot regiment. Richard Cannon compiled the record at the Adjutant General office, Horse Guards. Parker of London issued the pictured volume in eighteen fifty one. It gives the forming of the regiment in seventeen forty one.

Services of the South Devonshire regiment run from that date to eighteen fifty one. A general order of eighteen thirty six frames the whole record series. The king charged that services of every regiment be set in print. Formation, stations, battles, and sieges form the set heads of each account. Colours and trophies won by brave acts are to be specified there.
56293-historical-record-of-the-tenth-or-:
The Historical Record of the Tenth, or the North Lincolnshire, Regiment of Foot gives an account of the regiment's formation in 1685 and of its subsequent services to 1847. Richard Cannon, of the Adjutant General's office at Horse Guards, compiled it, and Parker printed it in London in 1847, with plates.

A set of general orders from Horse Guards, dated January 1, 1836, stands at the front and explains the whole series. The King had commanded that an account of the services of every regiment in the British Army be published. Each record must give the regiment's formation, its stations, its battles and sieges, and its captured colours and trophies. The names of officers and men killed, wounded, or distinguished in action are also required.
66459-historical-record-of-the-thirty-fo:
The Historical Record of the Thirty-Fourth Regiment of Foot gives the services of the Cumberland regiment. The volume appeared in London in 1844. It belongs to Richard Cannon's series of regimental histories. The Adjutant General's office directed the series by royal command. Plates illustrate the record.

General orders of 1836 open the book. The king commanded an account of every regiment's services. Each record must give the regiment's formation and stations. It must list battles, sieges, and captured trophies. It must name officers and men killed or wounded. It must record honours and badges with their causes. This volume covers the Thirty-Fourth from its formation in 1702 to 1844.
66614-historical-record-of-the-thirty-ni:
Historical Record of the Thirty-Ninth, or the Dorsetshire Regiment of Foot is an official army history compiled by Richard Cannon. It gives an account of the forming of the regiment in 1702 and of its services down to 1853. The work forms part of a series of historical records of the British Army issued by command from the Adjutant-General's office.

The title page of the series shows royal patronage, by command of the late King William the Fourth and under the patronage of the Queen. Cannon's task across the series was the same for every regiment in the service. He gathered the record of raising, campaigns, and service into one printed account. For the Thirty-Ninth, that means a century and a half of regimental life, from its first formation under Queen Anne to the middle of the reign of Victoria.
76297-the-constitutional-iniquity-involv:
Mrs Josephine E Butler wrote a pamphlet on the wrong, in law and in morals, of all state regulation of prostitution. The moral side is most weighty, she grants, but the legal and constitutional side is scarcely less so. She cites Professor Sheldon Amos of London University, who exposed the legal side in Laws for the Regulation of Vice. Mittermayer and Montesquieu stand as authorities on criminal law.

A penal code, Mittermayer says, is the keystone of a nation public law. On the words of Montesquieu rests the claim that liberty of the subject turns on good criminal laws. The regulation system, Butler argues, is severe penal law in disguise. It builds an arbitrary tribunal for offences invented by its own makers, she holds. New crimes draw new and terrible penalties unheard of in the country. Reformers get a legal case against the Contagious Diseases Acts system.
britannica-1911-oleg:
Oleg, who died in 912, was a prince of Kiev. An entry in the 1911 Encyclopaedia Britannica tells how he built early Rus power. He followed Rurik as head of the ruling house at Novgorod. Three years later he moved south and took Kiev as his capital.

Oleg raised a fort at Kiev and forced nearby tribes to pay tribute. His raids broke the hold of the Khazars in the south. In 907 he sailed against Constantinople with a great fleet. The Greeks paid tribute and signed a formal pact with his envoys. A fuller treaty in 911 opened free trade between the two peoples. Oleg died at Kiev in 912 and was buried there.
britannica-1911-thalweg: Thalweg is a German word used in the study of land forms. It joins the words for valley and way. The term names the line of steepest slope along the floor of a valley. That line runs through the lowest points as the valley falls. It thus marks the path that a stream will take. The entry is a very brief note from the nineteen eleven reference work, and it gives just the sense of the term and where it comes from.
doe-osti-17198173-nonlinear-data-compres:
Sandia National Laboratories report SAND2026-27128R, printed in September 2026, presents R. Loek Van Heyningen's work on shrinking simulation data by first aligning it. The method, called image registration, learns a smooth, reversible warp of the domain so that moving features in separate simulation fields line up. Aligned fields can then be squeezed into a small set of basis patterns, which cheaper reduced models are trained on.

Two approaches are developed for bounded domains, where the warp must not distort the shape of the domain. One builds the map from radial basis functions in a layered, composed scheme that guards the boundary. The other follows a vector flow with a constrained kernel that limits which maps are allowed. Both are tested on two- and three-dimensional transient problems and on steady aerodynamic data over curved and non-convex domains.
doe-osti-3002144-tasti-grid-overview-of-:
Hillary Fishler, Varisara Tansakul, and Supriya Chinthavali of Oak Ridge present a slide deck, ORNL/LTR-2025/4000, on Oregon's power grid. The deck introduces TASTI-GRID, a national tool that helps states and tribes decide where grid resilience money does the most good. It draws on more than 60 public data sets. Oregon is the worked example here.

Slides map Oregon's generation and transmission lines, substations, past major outages, and extreme weather impacts. Other slides cover customer demographics, meter types, and whether energy rates stay affordable. The deck closes with steps for small towns and rural cooperatives, such as gradual metering upgrades with incentives. State energy offices use this kind of overview before they commit funds to harden the grid against storms.
doe-osti-3097328-los-alamos-innovation-e:
Los Alamos National Laboratory tells a tech transfer story in report LA-UR-26-23101, issued April 15, 2026, under Dharmesh N. Patel. Lab researchers built a porous sorbent that pulls carbon dioxide from air with little energy. A firm named Spiritus licensed the material, which anchors its Carbon Orchard approach to direct air capture. The sorbent now sits at the heart of a much larger build-out planned in Wyoming.

Spiritus joined a 500 million dollar partnership with Prometheus Hyperscale and Casper Carbon Capture. Their Casper, Wyoming project pairs permanent carbon removal with advanced computing plants, billing the result as one of the largest carbon-negative digital infrastructure projects in the world. The sheet frames the deal as proof that lab materials work can scale into heavy industry.
govdocs-archive_org-nsia-RaserGreg_Raser: Greg Raser wrote this letter by hand to Harold Weisberg in April 1994. Handwritten letters fill the later years of Weisberg's mail, from readers and researchers who had followed his books for decades. The file keeps the letter under Raser's name and its date. It does not summarize what Raser wrote, so the letter's news or requests cannot honestly be described beyond its place in that correspondence.
new-york-times-current-history-the-europ:
The New York Times issued this number of its Current History magazine on the European War. It covers the start of the war to March 1915. Its theme is set as a question: Who Began the War, and Why? The contents begin with the case for Germany.

Speeches by Kaiser Wilhelm the Second fill much of the number. He forgives enemies, speaks from the throne, and addresses the German army and navy. Other pieces cheer the men as one for the Kaiser, hearts for God and fists on the enemy. His letter to Lord Tweedmouth is also printed. Readers in America could weigh Germany's own words early in the war.
podcast-tuckercarlson-JS-3QssVPeg:
Economist Jeffrey Sachs joins Tucker Carlson to give what the title calls the untold history. It covers the Cold War as he reconstructs it, and the CIA coups that punctuated it around the world. It also covers the origin of Covid. On that subject Sachs has broken publicly with the official account he once helped administer.

Sachs chaired the Lancet's Covid commission and emerged convinced the virus likely came from laboratory work, a position he argues here alongside his longer indictment of American foreign policy. Carlson, an eager host for both arguments, lets him build the full arc. Sachs's views are contested by many former colleagues; his standing makes the contest significant. The episode preserves a pillar of the establishment prosecuting the establishment, in detail, which is a rarer document than any outsider's critique.
